extracted.intended_audience: media researchers, journalism scholars, and computational-journalism practitioners studying news selection, bias audits, and newsworthiness
extracted.subtask_description: Methodological guidance for studying news selection and measuring media bias by comparing media output to independent, extra‑media benchmarks (e.g., event statistics), including comparative and cross‑national designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra-Media Benchmark
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare news coverage of an event class to an independent, statistical measure of how often that class actually occurs; bias is the deviation between the two, not coverage frequency itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use independent statistics about events (the 'extra-media' data) as a baseline. Example: Rosengren used the actual list of parliamentary elections held as the benchmark against which newspaper coverage was compared. Interpret over- or under-representation relative to that benchmark as evidence of selection bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population Definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the universe of potential news events before coding, not from the news itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify (a priori) the full population of events that could have been reported (e.g., all national parliamentary elections in a given period) to avoid circularity where the news determines what counts as an event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event-Type Operationalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Code events by attributes whose distribution in the world is independently knowable (e.g., elections, country wealth, military spending) so that coverage can be benchmarked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose event classifications and attributes that have external, measurable data sources so you can compare world supply to media selection. This supports valid statistical comparison and controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple Outlets, Multiple Countries
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare coverage across outlets and countries to separate idiosyncratic editor choice from systematic news values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross‑national and multi‑outlet designs help distinguish local editorial preferences from broader structural selection effects. Include a range of media systems and outlets to identify systematic patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real-World Event Frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Story selection should be benchmarked against the frequency of relevant event classes; over-representation indicates a value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure how often different types of events occur in the world and compare to their news frequency; a higher share in the news than in the world indicates a news value favoring that event type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Country Salience Independent of News
rubrics_metrics.description: Population, GDP, treaty memberships, geographic proximity should be measurable independently and treated as covariates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include independent measures of country size, wealth, political ties, and proximity when modeling coverage to separate intrinsic salience from editorial selection. Treat these as expected supply-related predictors rather than outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source Country's Media Capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage flows from countries with developed news infrastructure (and English-language wires); this is supply, not demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for differential availability of news from countries with strong media systems and wire services; higher coverage from these countries may reflect supply-side advantages rather than newsroom preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/Political Affinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Net of size, allied/like-system countries get more coverage than rivals — a selection bias based on cultural or political affinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model alliance, ideological similarity, or system likeness as predictors of coverage. Rosengren found allied countries received more attention even when other factors were controlled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproportionate Coverage of Elite Nations
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers tend to give disproportionate coverage to elite nations even controlling for whether relevant events (e.g., elections) were happening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test for over-representation of high‑status or elite countries relative to the extra‑media distribution of events; treat such disproportion as evidence of status-based news values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic Bias Beyond Proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographic bias exists that cannot be fully explained by simple proximity measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine spatial patterns in coverage after controlling for distance; residual geographic biases indicate other selection mechanisms (political ties, cultural affinity, historical relations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty/Alliance-System Bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Elections in allied countries got more coverage than elections in non-allied countries with similar populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include alliance/treaty membership variables when benchmarking coverage; identify whether political relationships predict excess coverage beyond material covariates like population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-Outlet, Single-Country Studies Are Insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-outlet, single-country studies are insufficient to identify news values; benchmarks are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid drawing general conclusions about news values from single‑newsroom or single‑country analyses without external baselines and comparative cases; such designs conflate supply and selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: News Values Are Conditional on Supply
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported 'negativity' or other apparent news values may reflect the world's supply of events (e.g., more negative events occurred) rather than a newsroom preference, unless extra-media data say otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret observed news attributes (negativity, personalization, elite focus) conditional on the distribution of those attributes in the event population. Use extra‑media data to adjudicate whether newsroom selection or world supply drives patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias Measurement Requires Baselines
rubrics_metrics.description: Bias measurement requires baselines: Any modern audit (homepage placement, recommender systems) inherits Rosengren's demand for an independent reference distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When auditing media (including algorithms and homepages), specify and justify an independent baseline distribution of events or content; measure deviations from that baseline to quantify bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct Counterfactual Baselines (Anticipates Causal-Inference Critiques)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses should construct counterfactual baselines to support causal claims about selection — anticipating modern causal‑inference concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design studies that enable counterfactual reasoning (what would have been covered if supply were uniform?) and apply causal‑inference logic when attributing selection effects to news values rather than supply differences.
